title: Ember Appalachian Stack Cake
summary: Thin molasses cake layers stacked with glazed dried-apple filling — rested overnight so it all melds.
story: The stack cake is the mountain celebration cake. Tradition says neighbors each brought a layer to a gathering and the host stacked them with apple filling between — the more layers, the more loved you were. The secret is the overnight rest: the filling soaks into the cake and the whole thing turns into something no single layer could be.

steps.title: Make the filling
steps.body: Simmer the dried apples in water until soft, about 30 minutes. Stir in the sugar, cinnamon, and nutmeg and cook until thick and glossy. Cool.

steps.title: Bake the layers
steps.body: Mix the dry ingredients. Cream the molasses, butter, and eggs, then alternate adding dry mix and buttermilk. Divide among 5–6 greased 9-inch pans (thin layers!) and bake at 350°F for 12–15 minutes.

steps.title: Stack
steps.body: Spread apple filling between every layer while the cake is still slightly warm. Don't frost the top — stack cake wears its layers proud.

steps.title: Rest
steps.body: Cover and rest overnight at room temperature. This isn't optional — the filling needs the night to soak in.

proTips: Thin layers are the whole game — thick cake layers won't absorb the filling.
Sorghum molasses is the traditional sweetener if you can find it.

title: Ember Kentucky Hot Brown
summary: Toast piled with turkey, drowned in Mornay sauce, topped with tomato and bacon, broiled bubbly. Use smoked turkey and it's a new animal.
story: Born at the Brown Hotel in Louisville in 1926, invented for the late-night dance crowd. It's Kentucky's most famous sandwich — open-faced turkey under a blanket of cheese sauce with bacon crossed on top. The Ember twist: use smoked turkey instead of plain roast, and the whole thing picks up a backbone the original never had.

items: 1 lb sliced turkey (smoked if you've got it)

steps.title: Make the Mornay
steps.body: Melt the butter, whisk in the flour, and cook 2 minutes. Slowly whisk in the milk and simmer until thick. Off the heat, stir in both cheeses, nutmeg, salt, and white pepper until smooth.

steps.title: Build
steps.body: Lay toast in an oven-safe dish. Pile on the turkey, ladle over a generous amount of Mornay, and top with tomato slices.

steps.title: Broil
steps.body: Broil 3–5 minutes until the sauce is bubbly and spotted golden. Top with crossed bacon strips, a dusting of paprika, and parsley. Serve immediately.

proTips: Smoked turkey is the move — it turns a hotel classic into a barbecue dish.
Keep the Mornay moving while it simmers or it'll catch on the bottom.

title: Ember Vinegar Pie
summary: The Depression-era miracle — a custard pie with no fruit that tastes like lemon chess pie.
story: When mountain winters meant no fresh fruit, cooks reached for what they had: vinegar. Apple cider vinegar gives this custard the bright tang of lemon, and nobody believes there's no lemon in it until you show them the recipe. Dust it with nutmeg and serve it proud.

steps.title: Mix
steps.body: Whisk the sugar and flour, then whisk in the eggs, vinegar, melted butter, and vanilla until smooth.

steps.title: Bake
steps.body: Pour into the pie crust and bake at 350°F for 40–45 minutes, until the center is just set with a slight jiggle.

steps.title: Finish
steps.body: Cool completely, dust with nutmeg, and slice. Serve at room temperature.

proTips: Don't overbake — the center should still tremble slightly when it comes out.
Apple cider vinegar is the classic; white vinegar works but tastes sharper.

title: Ember Shoofly Pie
summary: Dark molasses custard under a brown-sugar crumb top — the most iconic Amish dessert there is.
story: Shoofly pie is Pennsylvania Dutch country on a plate, and the Amish settlements in Kentucky carry the tradition too. Gooey molasses on the bottom, cake-like crumbs on top. Kelly's made this one before, so it had to be right.

items: ½ cup butter, cold and cubed

steps.title: Make the crumbs
steps.body: Cut the butter into the flour and brown sugar until it looks like coarse crumbs. Set aside.

steps.title: Mix the filling
steps.body: Stir the baking soda into the hot water, then whisk in the molasses.

steps.title: Assemble
steps.body: Pour the molasses mixture into the pie crust. Sprinkle two-thirds of the crumbs over the top, then the rest — the layers settle into gooey and cakey as it bakes.

steps.title: Bake
steps.body: Bake at 350°F for 40–45 minutes until the center is just set. Cool completely before slicing.

proTips: Don't overbake — the center should tremble slightly; it sets as it cools.
Serve at room temperature, never warm — the layers need to settle.

title: Ember Amish Chicken Corn Soup
summary: Golden chicken broth with sweet corn and rivels — the little flour dumplings that make it Amish.
story: This is the soup of Pennsylvania Dutch country, ladled at church suppers and family tables. Rivels are nothing but flour, egg, and salt rubbed into little pebbles and dropped in the simmering broth — they puff into tender dumplings. Simple food, deeply comforting.

steps.title: Simmer the chicken
steps.body: Cover the chicken with water, bring to a boil, then simmer 60–90 minutes with the onion, carrots, and celery until the meat falls off the bone.

steps.title: Shred
steps.body: Pull the chicken out, shred the meat, and return it to the pot. Season the broth with salt and pepper. Stir in the corn.

steps.title: Make the rivels
steps.body: Rub the flour, egg, and salt together with your fingers into pea-sized bits.

steps.title: Drop and finish
steps.body: Bring the soup to a lively simmer and drop in the rivels. Cook 10 minutes until they float and turn tender. Serve hot.

proTips: Don't skip skimming the broth — clear golden soup starts with a clean pot.
Rivels should be pea-sized; bigger ones stay doughy in the middle.

title: Ember Whoopie Pies
summary: Chocolate cake rounds sandwiched with thick cream filling — Amish-born, everybody-loved.
story: The whoopie pie started in Amish kitchens — legend says farmers shouted 'whoopie!' when they found them in their lunch pails. Two soft chocolate cakes, a cloud of vanilla cream between them. Kids lose their minds; adults pretend they're for the kids.

steps.title: Bake the cakes
steps.body: Mix the dry ingredients. Cream the butter and sugar, beat in the egg and vanilla, then alternate adding dry mix and buttermilk. Drop rounded tablespoons onto lined baking sheets and bake at 350°F for 10–12 minutes.

steps.title: Make the filling
steps.body: Beat the butter, powdered sugar, marshmallow creme, and vanilla until fluffy.

steps.title: Assemble
steps.body: Sandwich the filling between pairs of cooled cakes. Let them set 30 minutes so they hold together.

proTips: Cool the cakes completely or the filling melts out the sides.
A scoop keeps the cakes even so the pairs match up.

title: Ember Old-Fashioned Potato Salad
summary: Mustardy, a little sweet, loaded with hard-boiled eggs — the old-fashioned potato salad Kelly grew up on.
story: This is the potato salad of church picnics and family reunions — mustard in the dressing, a spoon of sugar, hard-boiled eggs through and through, paprika on top. Kelly's always just called it old-fashioned potato salad, and that's exactly what it is.

steps.title: Cook the potatoes
steps.body: Boil the potatoes in salted water until just tender — 12–15 minutes. Drain and cool.

steps.title: Mix the dressing
steps.body: Stir the mayo, mustard, sugar, vinegar, salt, and pepper until smooth.

steps.title: Combine
steps.body: Fold the potatoes, eggs, celery, and onion into the dressing. Dust the top with paprika.

steps.title: Chill
steps.body: Refrigerate at least 2 hours — overnight is better. The flavors need time to marry.

proTips: Dress the potatoes while they're still slightly warm — they soak up more flavor.
Don't overcook the potatoes or it turns to mush. Just tender.

title: Kristy's Chicken and Dumplings
summary: Kristy's killer chicken and dumplings — whole chicken, flat dumplings from flour, lard, and milk, and a thick peppery broth.
story: This one's Kristy's. Whole chicken simmered down — smoked first if you're feeling it — with flat dumplings made her way: just flour, lard, and milk, rolled and cut in rectangles. No celery, no onions. The broth goes thick and peppery, and that's the whole point.

items: 1 whole chicken (3–4 lbs), smoked first if you like
Salt and plenty of black pepper

steps.title: Simmer the chicken
steps.body: Cover the chicken with water, bring to a boil, then simmer 60–90 minutes until the meat falls off the bone. Pull the chicken, shred the meat, and return it to the pot. Season boldly with salt and lots of black pepper.

steps.title: Thicken
steps.body: Let the broth reduce a little, or mash a spoonful of the chicken against the pot to help it along — Kristy's broth is thick, not thin.

steps.title: Make the dumplings
steps.body: Cut the lard into the flour and salt, stir in the milk just until it comes together. Roll thin and cut into rectangles.

steps.title: Drop and finish
steps.body: Lay the dumplings on the simmering broth — don't stir for the first 10 minutes or they'll break up. Simmer 15–20 minutes until tender. Serve in deep bowls with plenty of broth.

proTips: Smoke the chicken first if you want — it adds a backbone the plain version doesn't have.
Don't stir early. The dumplings need those first 10 minutes undisturbed to set.

title: Ember Datil Pepper BBQ Sauce
finish: Thick enough to coat a spoon
summary: St. Augustine's sweet-heat pepper in a tomato-molasses sauce — habanero heat with a fruity sweetness.
story: The datil pepper grows in St. Augustine, Florida, and nowhere else much cares — which is a shame, because it's one of the best hot peppers on earth. Habanero-level heat with a sweet, fruity flavor that plays beautifully with brown sugar and molasses. This is Florida in a jar.

steps.title: Sweat the aromatics
steps.body: Soften the onion, garlic, and datils in a splash of oil over medium heat, 5 minutes. Wear gloves with the datils — they're hot.

steps.title: Simmer
steps.body: Add everything else and simmer 30 minutes, stirring now and then, until thick enough to coat a spoon.

steps.title: Blend
steps.body: Blend smooth with an immersion blender. Taste and adjust — more datil for heat, more brown sugar for sweet, splash of vinegar to brighten.

steps.title: Jar it
steps.body: Cool and refrigerate. Keeps 3–4 weeks. The heat mellows a touch after a day or two.

proTips: Can't find fresh datils? Dried datils work — rehydrate in hot water first. Habaneros are the backup, but they're less sweet.
Start with 4 peppers. Datils run 100,000–300,000 Scoville — respect them.

title: Ember Mississippi Comeback Sauce
summary: The Jackson, Mississippi classic — creamy, peppery, a little tangy. Goes on everything.
story: Comeback sauce was born in Jackson, Mississippi, and every table in town has its own version. It's a remoulade-style dipping sauce — creamy, peppery, tangy — and once you try it on fries or fried pickles, you'll understand why they call it comeback. You'll keep coming back for more.

steps.title: Whisk
steps.body: Whisk everything together in a bowl until smooth and evenly pink.

steps.title: Chill
steps.body: Cover and refrigerate at least 2 hours — the flavors need time to marry. Overnight is even better.

steps.title: Serve
steps.body: Dip fries, fried pickles, chicken tenders, or onion rings. Spread it on burgers and po'boys. Keeps about a week in the fridge.

proTips: Grate the onion on the fine side of a box grater — you want the juice and pulp, not chunks.
The coarse black pepper is non-negotiable. It's what makes it comeback sauce.

title: Ember Jalapeño Popper Pork Loin Fatty
summary: A butterflied pork loin stuffed with jalapeño popper filling, rolled tight, wrapped in a bacon weave, and smoked.
story: Kelly's fatty isn't the sausage-log kind — it's a whole pork loin cut open and stuffed, the way he's always made it. This one's got a jalapeño popper filling: cream cheese, sharp cheddar, bacon, and jalapeños. The hard part of any stuffed loin is keeping the cheese inside, and the fix is all technique — a clean border, a tight roll, butcher's twine, a bacon weave, and 30 minutes in the freezer before it hits the smoke.

items: 3–4 jalapeños, diced (seeds out for mild, in for wild)

steps.title: Butterfly
steps.body: Butterfly the loin lengthwise into an even sheet about ¾ inch thick. Take your time and don't cut through.

steps.title: Stuff
steps.body: Spread the cream cheese edge to edge, leaving a 1-inch border all around. Layer on the cheddar, jalapeños, crumbled bacon, and green onions. That border is what seals the roll.

steps.title: Roll and tie
steps.body: Roll tight from the long side, tucking as you go. Tie with butcher's twine every 2 inches.

steps.title: Wrap
steps.body: Wrap in a bacon weave, seam-side down. Season the outside with rub.

steps.title: Freeze
steps.body: Freeze 30 minutes before smoking. Cold cheese melts slower — it sets instead of running out.

steps.title: Smoke
steps.body: Smoke at 250°F over apple or hickory to 145°F internal, about 2½–3 hours. Glaze with BBQ sauce in the last 30 minutes.

steps.title: Rest and slice
steps.body: Rest 15 minutes — the cheese firms up as it cools. Cut the twine and slice thick.

proTips: The six rules for no melt-out: border, tight roll, twine, bacon weave, freeze before smoking, rest after.
Seeds out = family friendly. Seeds in = wake-up call.

title: Ember Thor's Hammer
summary: A whole beef shank smoked like a brisket — deep bark, shreddable meat, and marrow in the bone.
story: Thor's hammer is a whole beef fore shank with the bone frenched clean so it looks like a hammer handle. It's all over social media for the drama, but it's a legitimately great eat — the shank is loaded with collagen that turns silky over a long, slow smoke. All savory here: heavy black pepper, garlic, and beef tallow. No sweet stuff.

items: 1 whole beef fore shank, 3–5 lbs, bone frenched clean
2 Tbsp beef tallow, for the wrap

steps.title: Season heavy
steps.body: Coat the shank in a thin layer of mustard, then season aggressively on all sides. A 4-pound hunk of meat can take the full rub — don't be shy.

steps.title: Smoke
steps.body: 250°F over oak or hickory. Spritz with the broth-Worcestershire mix every hour after the first 3 hours.

steps.title: Wrap
steps.body: When the bark is set and deep mahogany (around 165°F internal), wrap in butcher paper with the beef tallow.

steps.title: Cook to tender
steps.body: Go to probe-tender, 203–205°F — the probe should slide in like butter. Plan on 8–10 hours total. If it's tough, it needs more time, not more heat.

steps.title: Rest
steps.body: Rest wrapped in a cooler at least 1 hour.

steps.title: Shred and serve
steps.body: Shred the meat, spoon the marrow out of the bone, and mix it right in. Serve on toasted rolls or over mashed potatoes.

proTips: Ask the butcher to french the bone for you — most will do it free.
The marrow is the cook's treat. Don't let anyone talk you out of it.
